lead.text: Size is the main thing a team controls about a pull request. A reviewer can hold a hundred lines in mind and judge whether they are right, but with a thousand lines the reading becomes skimming, and mistakes pass through. A small change can also be reverted on its own, where a large one takes all its good parts with it.
A good pull request does one thing, has a short description of what and why, and has passing checks.

lead.text: **GitHub flow** is the pattern described earlier in this lesson: branch from `main`, push, open a pull request, review, merge, and deploy. Main is always in a state that could go live, and each branch lives until its pull request is merged. It suits a team that ships one hosted version of a product again and again.

**Trunk-based development** pushes the same idea further. Developers merge small changes to one main branch, called the trunk, at least daily, and any branch lives for a day or two at most. That raises a question: how can half-finished work be merged without breaking the product? The usual answer is a **feature flag**, a switch in the code that keeps new behaviour hidden until it is ready, so that the code can be merged long before the feature is turned on.

afterFigure.text: The point of both is to keep branches short, because the cost of a branch is not in creating it, which is instant, but in how long it stays apart from main.

lead.text: Not every product has a single live version. A library may have users on version 2.x who need security fixes while version 3.x is under active development, and for such a case a team keeps a long-lived **release branch** for each supported version, and applies fixes to each of them separately.

A well-known description of this approach is Vincent Driessen's 'A successful Git branching model', published in January 2010. He later added a note to the article saying that it suits software that is released in explicit versions, and is a poor fit for web applications that are delivered continuously.

It is a switch in the code, and the word names the kind of marker it is.

lead.text: A team that depends on review can ask the hosting service to enforce it. A **protected branch** refuses direct pushes, and accepts a merge only when the rules are met, for example that the tests pass and that at least one other person has approved.

The rules are a team's decision and not a Git feature, but they make the earlier advice enforceable, and checks are what let a reviewer concentrate on design and leave the mechanical errors to the machine.

lessons.orientation: Compare trunk-based development, GitHub flow and long-lived release branches, and say what a pull request is for.
lessons.nextAction: Mark releases with tags and version numbers, and write messages that others can use.

blocks.text: Git places no limit on how a team uses it. It will let anyone with access push straight to `main`, leave a branch unmerged for six months, or merge a change of a thousand lines that no one else has read. A team that wants to avoid those outcomes has to agree a **workflow** on top of Git, a shared habit about how long branches live, how changes are reviewed and what a release looks like.

What matters in a workflow is how long a branch stays apart from main, because the longer it does, the more there is to review, the more is likely to conflict and the harder a mistake is to take back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a pull request is for, and choose a workflow for a described team.
intro.whyItMatters: Branches cost almost nothing in Git, and the workflow decides what they cost a team.

recap.keyIdea: A pull request is a hosting service's way of reviewing a branch before it is merged, and workflows differ mainly in how long branches live.

blocks.text: A pull request carries a branch through review and automatic checks before it is merged, and it is a feature of hosting services, not of Git. Small, focused pull requests are faster to review, cause fewer conflicts and can be reverted alone.

GitHub flow keeps a deployable main and short-lived branches, trunk-based development merges daily and hides unfinished work behind feature flags, and release branches serve products that must support several versions at once. Protected branches make the review and check rules binding.

lessons.title: Tags, versions and messages

reveal.text: A commit moves the branch that HEAD is on, as the lesson on branches showed, and a tag is not a branch, so it stays where it was put.

lead.text: A branch label moves forward with every commit made on it, which is useless for saying *this exact commit is version 1.0*. A **tag** is the answer: a name attached to one commit that never moves. Create it on the commit you release, with `git tag v1.0`, and it will name that commit for ever.

Git has two kinds of tag. A **lightweight tag** is only a pointer, like a branch that never moves, and `git cat-file -t` on it reports `commit`, because the name points straight at a commit. An **annotated tag**, made with `git tag -a v1.0 -m` followed by a message, is a real object of its own that records who tagged it, when, and with what message, and `git cat-file -t` reports `tag`.

afterFigure.text: Tags are only local until pushed. `git push` does not send them by default, and `git push origin v1.0` sends one.

diagram.alt: A line of commits with a branch label main and a tag label v1.0. In the first view both labels are on the same commit. After two more commits main has moved to the newest commit and v1.0 stays on the old one.

lead.text: Once releases have names, the names should carry meaning. **Semantic Versioning**, described at semver.org, gives each of the three numbers a job. The **patch** number goes up for a backwards-compatible bug fix. The **minor** number goes up for new functionality that is backwards compatible, and the patch number then goes back to zero. The **major** number goes up for a change that breaks existing users, and the minor and patch numbers then both go back to zero.
The point of the scheme is that a user reading only the number can tell what an upgrade risks: a patch should be safe to take, a minor should add without breaking, and a major needs care.

afterFigure.text: The left-hand number always outranks the right, and a bump resets everything to its right.

diagram.alt: A version number split into MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH boxes. The starting version is 2.4.1. A bug fix gives 2.4.2, a compatible feature gives 2.5.0, and a breaking change gives 3.0.0, with the changed boxes highlighted.
diagram.caption: A change of the left-hand number outranks one on the right, and it resets what lies to its right to zero. Use the buttons to apply each kind of change.

steps.headline: Start from 1.7.4 and apply a fix, a compatible feature and a breaking change, in that order.

workedSteps.text: A backwards-compatible fix raises the patch number.
A compatible feature raises the minor number and resets the patch number to zero.
A breaking change is made next.

reveal.text: A lightweight tag points straight at a commit, so `git cat-file -t` shows the commit's type. An annotated tag is an object in its own right and prints `tag`.

lead.text: The diff already records *what* changed, line by line, so the useful part of a commit message is the *why*: what problem the change solves, and why this approach. The conventional layout is a short summary line, a blank line, and then a body for the reason.

Some teams also write the summary in a machine-readable form. The **Conventional Commits** format begins each message with a type such as `feat` or `fix`, an optional scope in brackets, a colon and the summary, and marks a breaking change with an exclamation mark or a `BREAKING CHANGE` footer. Because a `feat` means a minor bump, a `fix` a patch bump and a breaking change a major bump, tools can read the messages since the last tag and choose the next version number themselves.

diagram.alt: A commit message laid out as a summary line, a blank line and a body. The first view shows a plain message whose body gives the reason. The second view shows a Conventional Commits message with a type, a scope and a breaking-change footer.
diagram.caption: A reader sees the summary first and the body only if they look further. Use the buttons to compare a plain message with a Conventional Commits message.

reveal.text: The diff already shows which lines changed. What does it not show?

lead.text: Some files do not belong in a repository: logs, build output, local settings, and above all secrets such as passwords and keys. A file named **.gitignore** lists patterns, such as `*.log`, for files that Git should treat as invisible. A new file matching a pattern never shows up as untracked, and `git add` will not stage it unless you force it.

The ignore rule has a limit that surprises people. It affects only *untracked* files. A file that is already tracked stays tracked after you add its name to `.gitignore`, and later edits to it still appear in `git status`. The same persistence applies to secrets. If a password was committed and pushed, deleting it in the next commit leaves it in every earlier commit and in every clone, so it cannot be taken back. The safe response is to treat it as exposed and change it, which is called rotating the secret, and cleaning the history is a second, optional step.

reveal.text: An ignored file does not appear in the untracked list.
The old password remains in the earlier commit and in every clone, so the secret has to be replaced. Replacing an exposed secret is called rotating it.

lessons.orientation: Name releases with tags and semantic versions, write commit messages others can use, and keep secrets and generated files out.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read and predict Git: status, history, branches, merges, rewrites, undo, remotes and releases. Apply that to your own repository.

blocks.text: A release of a program is one particular commit, and a project that has shipped version 2.4.1 has to be able to say which commit that is. Git provides a name for this purpose, the **tag**, and semantic versioning adds a convention for what the numbers inside such a name should mean, so that a version number tells a user what an upgrade is likely to change.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a tag is, bump a version correctly, write a message that gives a reason, and respond to a leaked secret.
intro.whyItMatters: A history is only useful later if its releases are named and its messages say why.

recap.keyIdea: A tag names one commit for ever, semantic versioning gives its numbers a meaning, messages should say why, and a pushed secret has to be treated as exposed.

blocks.text: A tag is a name that does not move, annotated tags are objects of their own, and a version number written as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH says whether a release is a fix, a compatible feature or a breaking change, with the numbers to the right reset to zero when one on the left goes up.

A good commit message gives a summary and the reason, and Conventional Commits makes the type readable by tools. A .gitignore hides untracked files and does nothing for tracked ones, and a password that has been pushed stays in the history, so it must be changed.

questions.prompt: A folder holds `report.docx`, `report_v2.docx`, `report_v3.docx`, `report_final.docx` and `report_final_REAL.docx`. What do the file names tell you about how the versions differ?
hints: Read the names as a stranger would, and ask what you could infer about `report_v3` from its name alone.
A name can put files in an order. Ask whether it can also describe a difference between two of them.

acceptedIdeas: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed

questions.onCorrect: A name identifies a file but cannot hold a description of a change, which is what a commit message is for.

misconceptions.feedback: A name such as `report_v2` says only that the file is a later copy. Nothing in it describes a change.
Nothing in a name such as `report_v3` records an author or a time.
Names such as v2, v3 and final do hint at an order, so calling them arbitrary goes further than the names justify.

choices.label: The names suggest an order, but say nothing about what changed
The names list the changes made in each version
The names record who made each version and when
The names are arbitrary, so they give no sign of which version came last

questions.prompt:
A teammate runs `git log --oneline` in a small project and gets this.

`3a4bb5d Fix the date format`
`06d39e4 Add the export button`
`712b543 Add the report page`

Which commit records no parent?
hints: The log lists the newest commit first. Which end of the list is the first commit that was ever made?
A parent is the commit that was current when this one was made.

acceptedIdeas: `712b543`, because nothing came before it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `712b543`, because nothing came before it

questions.onCorrect: Each commit points back to the one made before it, so the chain ends at the first commit, which is the only one with no parent.

choices.label: `712b543`, because nothing came before it
`3a4bb5d`, because it is the newest commit
`06d39e4`, because it sits in the middle
None of them, because every commit records a parent

misconceptions.feedback: The newest commit has the longest chain behind it. It records `06d39e4` as its parent.
It records `712b543` as its parent, the commit that was current when it was made.
The first commit in a project is the exception. Nothing came before it, so it has no parent to record.

questions.prompt: You edit three files this morning without committing, and at noon the laptop's disk fails. You pushed your last commit to the hosting service yesterday. What can you get back from the hosting service?
hints: Ask what a commit is: something you create on purpose.
Edits that were never committed were never in the history.

acceptedIdeas: The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits

questions.onCorrect: A repository keeps the states you commit and share. Work that exists only in an uncommitted edit has no copy anywhere else.

misconceptions.feedback: Git records a state only when you commit, and it does not watch the files between commits.
The commits you pushed were copied to the hosting service, so that history survives there.
A hosting service holds only what was pushed to it, and uncommitted edits are never pushed.

choices.label: Nothing at all, because the whole history was on the failed disk
The morning's edits, if the hosting service is still online
The commits you pushed yesterday, but not the morning's edits
The morning's edits, because Git tracks the files continuously

questions.prompt:
Each line of this log is one saved snapshot of the project, with a message and a link to the snapshot before it.

`3a4bb5d Fix the date format`
`06d39e4 Add the export button`

What does Git call a saved snapshot like this?
hints: It is also the word for the action of saving a snapshot with `git commit`.
The word is a noun here, one of the lines in the log.

acceptedIdeas: commit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A commit.

questions.onCorrect: A commit holds the whole project as it stood, a message, the author, the time and its parent.

misconceptions.feedback: Those words describe the idea, but Git has its own name for the saved snapshot that carries a message and a parent.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, "GitHub is down, so I can't look at last week's changes." She has a clone of the project on her laptop. What is wrong with what she says?
hints: Where did the commits go when she cloned the project?
Which parts of working with Git need the other machine, and which do not?

acceptedIdeas: Her clone holds the whole history, and Git reads it without GitHub
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her clone holds the whole history, and Git reads it without GitHub

questions.onCorrect: Git is the program and the history lives in the clone, so reading it works offline. GitHub only matters when commits are sent or fetched.

choices.label: Nothing: GitHub is the program that keeps the history
Nothing: Git can read history only while it can reach a host
Git can read it, but only after she signs in to GitHub
Her clone holds the whole history, and Git reads it without GitHub

misconceptions.feedback: GitHub hosts copies of repositories. The history is kept by Git, on her own disk, in the `.git` folder.
A clone includes every commit, so `git log` and `git show` work with no network at all.
Git does not need an account to read a repository on disk. A login matters only when she pushes or fetches.

questions.prompt: Ana pushed her project to a hosting service and Ben cloned it. The service then deletes the project by mistake. Ana's and Ben's laptops are untouched. What can they do?
hints: What does cloning download: the latest files or every commit?
Does a clone depend on the host to hold its history?

acceptedIdeas: Either one can push the full history to a new host
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Either one can push the full history to a new host

questions.onCorrect: Every clone is a complete repository, so any of them can seed a new host. That is what distributed means.

choices.label: Only Ana can, because she created the project
Either one can push the full history to a new host
Neither can, because the host held the only full copy
Either one can push the latest files, but the older commits are lost

misconceptions.feedback: Ben's clone holds the same complete history. Every clone is a full repository, whoever made the project.
A clone downloads every commit, so each laptop holds the history that the host held.
Older commits came down with the clone. The history is complete on every laptop.

questions.prompt:
You edit `a.txt` and create `notes.txt`, then run `git commit -am "Fix typo"`. Afterwards `git status --short` prints this.

`?? notes.txt`

What word does Git use for a file like `notes.txt`, which it has no record of?
hints: The two question marks are Git's way of saying it has never been told about the file.
The `-a` option stages only files Git already follows.

acceptedIdeas: untracked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Untracked.

questions.onCorrect: An untracked file stays out of every commit until you add it by name, even when you commit with `-a`.

misconceptions.feedback: A file can be new or unstaged and still be tracked. The word asked for describes a file Git has no record of.

questions.prompt: How many different versions of `a.txt` does Git hold at this moment, counting the working tree, the index and the last commit?
hints: Work out which version each place holds, using the lines above.
Compare them one by one: are any two of them equal?
Count the distinct version numbers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The working tree holds version 3, the index holds version 2 and the last commit holds version 1, so 3.

questions.onCorrect: `git add` copies content as it is at that moment, so edits made afterwards need adding again.

misconceptions.feedback: The working tree differs from the index as well, because of the second edit. All three places differ.
Three places each hold their own content, and here none of them agrees with another.

questions.prompt: You have staged two files and left a third edited but unstaged. Which command, with one option added to its plain form, shows only the changes in the two staged files?
hints: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index, so you need the other pair.
The option is a word with two dashes, and a synonym of it means the same as ready to be committed.

acceptedIdeas: git diff --cached
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git diff --cached (or --staged).

questions.onCorrect: `git diff --cached` compares the index with the last commit, which is exactly what `git commit` would record.

misconceptions.feedback: Plain `git diff` shows only the unstaged edits. An option on it switches to the staged ones.

questions.prompt: A tracked file `a.txt` has been edited, and a new file `new.txt` has never been added. You run `git commit -am` with a message. What does the new commit contain?
hints: Ask which of the two files Git already tracks.
`commit -a` stages tracked files and ignores untracked ones.

acceptedIdeas: The changes to `a.txt` only, with `new.txt` left out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The changes to a.txt only, with new.txt left out

questions.onCorrect: `new.txt` remains untracked after the commit, so a forgotten new file never sneaks in through `-a`, and has to be added by name.

misconceptions.feedback: The `-a` option stages changes to tracked files only, and `new.txt` is untracked, so it is not included.
Git commits as usual when untracked files are present, leaving them out and listing them as untracked afterwards.
The `-a` option does not add `new.txt`, and `a.txt` is tracked, so its edit is in the commit.

choices.label: Nothing, because git refuses to commit while an untracked file exists
The changes to both `a.txt` and `new.txt`
The changes to `a.txt` only, with `new.txt` left out
The new file `new.txt` only, because it is the newer change

questions.prompt: You have been working in a project all morning. In which state does `git status` leave each of these files?
hints: Ask two questions of each file: is its change in the index, and is the working tree different from the index?
A file Git has never been told about is neither staged nor unstaged.

items.label: You edit `a.txt` and run `git add a.txt`
items.explanation: The add copied the edit into the index, and nothing has changed since.

items.label: You create `new.txt` and run `git add new.txt`
items.explanation: Adding a new file puts it in the index, so the next commit will contain it.

items.label: You edit `b.txt` and run nothing else
items.explanation: The working tree differs from the index, and the index still matches the last commit.

items.label: You create `notes.txt` and run nothing else
items.explanation: Git has no earlier version of the file to compare, so it lists it as untracked.

items.label: You run `git add c.txt`, then edit `c.txt` again

No branch name at all

acceptedIdeas: The merge is paused, `config.ini` has markers and no commit exists yet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The merge is paused, `config.ini` has markers and no commit exists yet

questions.onCorrect: A conflicted merge stops half-way. You resolve the file, add it, and commit to finish, or abort to go back.

choices.label: The merge is paused, `config.ini` has markers and no commit exists yet
The merge finished and `config.ini` only needs a review
The merge was cancelled and nothing in the project changed
A merge commit was made with the conflict recorded in it

misconceptions.feedback: The merge did not finish. Git says the automatic merge failed and left the file for you to fix.
Nothing was cancelled. The working tree has the merge in progress, and `git merge --abort` is how you cancel it.
The commit comes last, after you resolve the file and run `git add` on it. Until then no merge commit exists.

questions.prompt: Your teammate has pulled all five commits of your branch. You run `git rebase -i HEAD~2`, reword the newest two, and force-push. What does your teammate meet on the next `git pull`?
hints: Which of the five commits have new hashes after the rebase?
Does your teammate's copy of those two commits appear in your branch?

acceptedIdeas: Their branch and yours have diverged, and their two old commits are not on yours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their branch and yours have diverged, and their two old commits are not on yours

questions.onCorrect: The first three commits are unchanged, but the last two were replaced. The teammate holds the old versions, so the histories have diverged.

choices.label: Their branch and yours have diverged, and their two old commits are not on yours
Nothing: the pull fast-forwards to your five commits
Nothing: Git sees the reworded commits as the same ones
Their repository is repaired, because the force-push deleted their commits too

misconceptions.feedback: Your last two commits are new copies. Their versions of those two are not ancestors of yours, so it cannot fast-forward.
A reworded commit has a new hash, so Git treats it as a different commit.
A force-push changes the branch on the host. It does not reach into anyone's repository.

questions.prompt: In the list that `git rebase -i HEAD~3` opens, a typo fix sits below the commit it belongs with. Which word do you put in front of the typo fix to fold it into the commit above?
hints: Think about which word combines a commit's change into the one above it.
The other words keep the commit separate, change only its message, or remove it.

acceptedIdeas: `squash`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `squash`

questions.onCorrect: Squashing folds the typo fix into the commit above, so two commits become one, and every commit from that line onward gets a new hash.

choices.label: `squash`
`reword`
`pick`
`drop`

misconceptions.feedback: `reword` keeps the commit separate and only lets you rewrite its message.
`pick` keeps the commit exactly as it is, so the typo fix would stay a separate commit.
`drop` removes the commit and its change completely, so the typo fix would be lost.

questions.prompt:
You run `git rebase main` on `feat` and Git stops. You fix `app.py`, delete the markers and run `git add app.py`. Git showed this when it stopped.

`CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py`
`error: could not apply b2659cc... Edit app`
`hint: Resolve all conflicts manually, mark them as resolved with`
`hint: "git add/rm <conflicted_files>", then run "git rebase --continue".`

What do you run next?
hints: Git's hint names the command that follows `git add`.
A rebase replays several commits, and it has more to replay after this one.

acceptedIdeas: `git rebase --continue`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `git rebase --continue`

questions.onCorrect: `git rebase --continue` records the resolved commit and replays the rest.

choices.label: `git rebase --continue`
`git commit`, as at the end of a merge
`git rebase main` again
`git merge --abort`

misconceptions.feedback: A commit alone leaves the rebase unfinished, and the commits after this one are never replayed. `--continue` makes the commit and carries on.
That would start a second rebase over a rebase already in progress. Git would refuse until you continue or abort.
There is no merge to abort here. To give up on a rebase you would use `git rebase --abort`.

questions.prompt: Commit `two` is gone from the branch after `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, and the reflog lists it as `HEAD@{1}`. Which command moves the branch forward to that commit again?
hints: Ask which command moves a branch to a commit you name.
One of these only lists positions, and another adds a new commit.

acceptedIdeas: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`

questions.onCorrect: The branch is back at `two` and `two.txt` returns, because the reflog kept the commit reachable by name.

choices.label: `git restore --source=HEAD@{1} .`
`git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`
`git revert HEAD@{1}`
`git reflog show HEAD@{1}`

misconceptions.feedback: That copies files from the commit into your working tree. It does not move the branch, so the branch would still lack `two`.
`git revert` adds a commit that reverses a change. Nothing needs reversing here, since the branch only has to move to a commit that still exists.
That only lists the reflog from that entry. It does not move the branch.

questions.prompt: You committed, but forgot to add `style.css`. The commit is only on your machine. Which command undoes the commit and leaves all of its changes staged, so you can add the file and commit again?
hints: All three reset modes move the branch back. They differ in what else they reset.
You want the index left as the removed commit had it.

acceptedIdeas: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`

questions.onCorrect: `--soft` moves only the branch, so the files stay staged exactly as the removed commit had them.

choices.label: `git reset --mixed HEAD~1`
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`
`git revert HEAD`

misconceptions.feedback: The mixed mode also resets the index, so the changes stay in your files but are no longer staged.
The hard mode resets the working tree as well, so the changes from the commit disappear from your files.
That adds a second commit that reverses the first. The commit would stay in the history.

questions.prompt: While `git bisect run` is searching, your test script exits with code 125 on one commit because the project does not build there. What does bisect do with that commit?
hints: Ask what the failure to build tells you about this commit.
Most codes mean good or bad, and one special code means neither.

acceptedIdeas: It skips the commit and tests another
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It skips the commit and tests another

questions.onCorrect: The code 125 tells bisect the commit cannot be tested, so it moves on to a neighbouring commit instead.

choices.label: It marks the commit bad
It stops the search with an error
It marks the commit good
It skips the commit and tests another

misconceptions.feedback: A code of 125 is not read as an ordinary failure.
Bisect carries on after a code it cannot use as good or bad.
Only an exit code of 0 means good, and a project that does not build is not good.

questions.prompt: The bug arrived at c6 among c1 to c8. Bisect tests c4 first, and a flaky test fails on it at random, so c4 is reported bad. What happens to the rest of the search?
hints: A bad result tells bisect that the first bad commit is at or before c4.
Ask whether c6 is in the half that is kept.

acceptedIdeas: It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6

questions.onCorrect: A test has to give the same answer every time on a given commit, or one wrong answer can send the search into the wrong half.

choices.label: It searches c5 to c8 and still finds c6
It tests c4 again, because the result contradicts itself
It searches c1 to c4, so it can never reach c6
It stops and reports an error

misconceptions.feedback: A bad result means the first bad commit is c4 or earlier, so bisect keeps the lower half. It cannot know the result was a fluke.
Bisect runs each test once and believes the result, so it sees no contradiction to check.
Bisect carries on, and the harm shows in the commit it finally reports.

questions.prompt: Tests passed at release `v1.2` and fail today. In what order do you run a manual bisect?
hints: Git cannot choose a middle commit until it knows both ends of the range.
Leave the session last, to get back to your branch.

items: Run `git bisect start`
Name the two ends with `git bisect bad` and `git bisect good v1.2`
Test the commit Git checks out and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`, repeating until Git names the first bad commit
Run `git bisect reset` to return to where you started

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Start the session, name the bad and the good ends, answer good or bad for each commit Git checks out until it names the culprit, and reset.

questions.onCorrect: Bisect needs a good end and a bad end before it can halve the range, and `git bisect reset` brings you back to your own branch.

questions.prompt: Your team's history has 3,000 commits since the last release that passed its tests. What is the largest number of tests `git bisect` needs to find the first bad commit?
hints: Find the smallest k with 2^k at least 3,000.
2^11 is 2,048, which is below 3,000, so the answer is the next exponent up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^11 is 2,048, which is too few, and 2^12 is 4,096, which is enough. So 12 tests are the most bisect needs.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve tests cover thousands of commits, because each test halves the range.

misconceptions.feedback: Eleven tests can separate 2,048 commits, which is fewer than 3,000.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, "Bisect needs 20 tests on a million commits, so on our two million it will need about 40." What is wrong with that?
hints: One extra test halves the range once more. How big a range does that cover?
Compare 2^20 with 2^21.

acceptedIdeas: Doubling the history adds one test, so about 21 would do
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doubling the history adds one test, so about 21 would do

questions.onCorrect: 2^20 is 1,048,576 and 2^21 is 2,097,152, so one extra test covers a history twice as long.

choices.label: Doubling the history adds one test, so about 21 would do
Nothing: the number of tests grows in proportion to the commits
Bisect always needs the same number of tests, whatever the size
It would need far more than 40, because bigger histories fail more often

misconceptions.feedback: Each test halves the range, so doubling the history costs one more halving and not double the tests.
The count does grow with size, but by one for every doubling.
How often a project fails does not change the search. It depends only on the number of commits.

questions.prompt: Your push is rejected with `fetch first`. You run `git fetch` and then `git push` again. What happens?
hints: The host accepts a push only if your branch contains everything the host has.
Ask what `git fetch` changes in your own repository.

acceptedIdeas: It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch

questions.onCorrect: The fetch brings the commits in, but your branch must still include them, by a merge or a rebase, before the host will accept it.

choices.label: It succeeds, because the fetch brought the host's commits into your branch
It is rejected again, because the fetch did not change your branch
It succeeds, because the fetch told the host which commits you have
It stops with a merge conflict, because the fetch merged the commits

misconceptions.feedback: A fetch updates `origin/main` and stores the commits, but it does not change your own branch.
The host does not need to be told. It checks whether your branch contains its current tip.
A fetch never merges. It changes nothing you are working on.

questions.prompt:
After a `git fetch`, `git status` prints this.

`On branch main`
`Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged,`
`and have 3 and 5 different commits each, respectively.`

How many commits does your `main` have that `origin/main` lacks?
hints: The first number belongs to your branch and the second to `origin/main`.
Commits your branch has that `origin/main` lacks are the ones a push would try to upload.
The sentence names your branch first and the remote branch second, so match each number to its branch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The status lists your branch's number first, so your `main` has 3 commits that `origin/main` lacks, and `origin/main` has 5 that your `main` lacks.

questions.onCorrect: The two numbers are the two sides of the fork. A merge or a rebase has to bring the five in before the three can be pushed.

misconceptions.feedback: Five is the number of commits `origin/main` has that your branch lacks. The first number belongs to your branch.
The two numbers count different commits on the two sides of the fork, so they are not added together here.

questions.prompt: A 1,000-line change was shipped as ten pull requests, merged one after another. Pull request 4 has a bug, and pull requests 5 to 10 do not touch its lines. You revert pull request 4. Which pull requests' changes are in `main` afterwards?
hints: A revert undoes one change by adding a new commit.
Ask which pull requests touch the lines that were reverted.

acceptedIdeas: Pull requests 1 to 3 and 5 to 10
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pull requests 1 to 3 and 5 to 10

questions.onCorrect: Had the change shipped as one pull request, the revert would have undone every line, good or bad.

choices.label: Pull requests 1 to 3 only
Pull requests 1 to 3 and 5 to 10
Pull requests 5 to 10 only
All ten, because a merged pull request cannot be reverted

misconceptions.feedback: A revert adds a commit that reverses one change. It does not roll the branch back, so pull requests 5 to 10 stay.
Pull requests 1 to 3 came before the bug, and the revert does not touch them.
Revert works on any commit in the history, and merged work is exactly what it is used for.

questions.prompt: The version is 1.8.0 and a breaking change is made. What is the new version?
hints: A breaking change raises the leftmost number.
A bump resets every number to its right to zero.
questions.onCorrect: The major number rose by one and the other two went back to zero, so 1.8.0 became 2.0.0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the patch bump for a bug fix. A breaking change raises the major number.
That is the minor bump for a compatible feature.
The major number does rise, but a bump resets every number to its right to zero.

questions.prompt: `git cat-file -t v1.0` prints `commit`. What kind of tag is `v1.0`?
hints: Think about what the name points at.
A tag with its own message and tagger is an object of its own, with its own type.

acceptedIdeas: A lightweight tag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A lightweight tag

questions.onCorrect: A lightweight tag is only a pointer, so the type shown is that of the commit it names.

choices.label: An annotated tag
A lightweight tag
A branch
A tag that has not been pushed

misconceptions.feedback: An annotated tag is an object of its own, so `git cat-file -t` prints a different type for it.
The question already calls `v1.0` a tag, so the choice is between the two kinds of tag.
Whether a tag has been pushed is a separate matter. `git cat-file -t` reports only the type of the object the name points at.

questions.prompt: A command-line tool is at version 2.4.1. Which part of the number goes up for each of these changes?
hints: Ask whether someone who upgrades without reading anything would be broken.
New things that break nobody are minor. Fixes that add nothing are patches.

items.label: Fix a crash when the input file is empty
items.explanation: A backwards-compatible bug fix raises the patch number.

items.label: Add an optional `--json` flag
items.explanation: New functionality that does not break existing use raises the minor number.

items.label: Remove the `--legacy` option that users depend on
items.explanation: Removing something users rely on breaks them, so the major number goes up.

items.label: Correct a typo in an error message
items.explanation: It is a compatible fix with no new functionality.

items.label: Add a new `export` command and leave the others as they are
items.explanation: It is a compatible addition.

items.label: Change the output format so scripts that read it stop working
items.explanation: Existing users are broken, which is what a major version signals.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The crash fix and the typo are patches, the `--json` flag and the `export` command are minor, and removing `--legacy` and changing the output format are major.

questions.onCorrect: The number tells a user how risky the upgrade is: a patch fixes, a minor adds, and a major may break.

questions.prompt:
`.env` was committed months ago. You add `.env` to `.gitignore`, edit the file, and run `git status --short`.

 `M .env`

Why is `.env` still listed?
hints: Ignore rules are about files Git has no record of. Does Git have a record of this one?
`git rm --cached .env` takes a file out of the index and leaves it on disk.

acceptedIdeas: The ignore rule covers untracked files, and `.env` is already tracked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ignore rule covers untracked files, and `.env` is already tracked

questions.onCorrect: A file that is already tracked stays tracked until you remove it from the index with `git rm --cached`.

choices.label: The ignore rule covers untracked files, and `.env` is already tracked
`.gitignore` takes effect only after a restart of Git
The pattern is wrong, so Git does not see it as ignored
Ignored files are always listed, with an M for each edit

misconceptions.feedback: Git reads `.gitignore` each time. The rule just does not apply to files it already follows.
The pattern `.env` is fine for a new file of that name. The file in question is tracked.
Ignored files are normally left out of the status. A tracked file is different, because Git still follows it.

flashcards.front: Why can a clone of a Git repository show you the history without contacting the server?
flashcards.back: Every clone contains the complete history, not only the latest files.

flashcards.front: In a project's log, which commit records no parent, and why?
flashcards.back: The first commit ever made, because nothing came before it. Every other commit records the one before it as its parent.

flashcards.front: What one word describes version control where every clone holds the full history?
flashcards.back: Distributed: the history is spread across every clone.

acceptedIdeas: distributed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distributed: the history is spread across every clone.

flashcards.front: Which command copies a file's content into the index?
flashcards.back: git add stages the content as it is at that moment, not the file for all time.

acceptedIdeas: git add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git add stages the content as it is at that moment, not the file for all time.

flashcards.front: Why does a file that was added and then edited show `MM` in `git status --short`?
flashcards.back: The left M compares the index with the last commit and the right M compares the working tree with the index, and both differ.

flashcards.front: What is the working tree's partner place that holds the draft of the next commit called?
flashcards.back: The index, also known as the staging area, holds the draft of the next commit.

acceptedIdeas: index
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The index, also known as the staging area, holds the draft of the next commit.

flashcards.front: Why do two files with the same text, in different folders, share one blob?
flashcards.back: A blob is named by the hash of its content alone, so identical content has one name and is stored once.

flashcards.front: Which object type holds the contents of one file and no name?
flashcards.back: A blob stores only contents, and the name is held by the tree that lists it.

acceptedIdeas: blob
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A blob stores only contents, and the name is held by the tree that lists it.

flashcards.front: Why does changing an old commit change the hash of every later commit?
flashcards.back: Each commit contains its parent's hash, so a changed parent changes the content, and so the hash, of its child.

flashcards.front: Which notation names the parent of the commit you are on?
flashcards.back: HEAD~1 is one step back along the parent links.

acceptedIdeas: HEAD~1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HEAD~1 is one step back along the parent links.

flashcards.front: What does main..feature select?
flashcards.back: The commits reachable from feature that are not reachable from main.

flashcards.front: Which command shows who last changed each line of a file?
flashcards.back: git blame prints each line with the commit that last touched it.

acceptedIdeas: git blame
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git blame prints each line with the commit that last touched it.

flashcards.front: What does the file .git/HEAD usually contain?
flashcards.back: It names the current branch, in a line such as ref: refs/heads/main.

flashcards.front: What is a branch, in terms of files?
flashcards.back: A small file naming one commit by its hash, so a branch is a pointer and not a copy.

flashcards.front: You delete a branch with `git branch -D`. What have you deleted, and what is left?
flashcards.back: You deleted the name, which is a small file holding a hash. The commits stay as objects until Git cleans up what nothing reaches.

flashcards.front: What is the common ancestor from which a three-way merge starts called?
flashcards.back: The merge base is the latest commit that both branches can reach.

acceptedIdeas: merge base
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The merge base is the latest commit that both branches can reach.

flashcards.front: What does Git print when a merge only moves a branch label forward, and what does it print when it makes a merge commit?
flashcards.back: A fast-forward prints `Fast-forward` and makes no commit. A merge commit prints `Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.`

flashcards.front: When does Git have to make a merge commit instead of a fast-forward?
flashcards.back: When the branch you merge into has commits of its own, so neither tip is an ancestor of the other.

flashcards.front: Which two letters does `git status --short` print beside a file whose merge conflict is unresolved?
flashcards.back: UU means the file is unmerged on both sides.

acceptedIdeas: UU
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UU means the file is unmerged on both sides.

flashcards.front: Why do edits to lines 2 and 3 of a file conflict even though no line was edited twice?
flashcards.back: Git merges in hunks, and changes that touch or abut count as one place where the histories disagree.

flashcards.front: Which command abandons a merge that stopped on a conflict?
flashcards.back: `git merge --abort` returns the project to its state before the merge.

acceptedIdeas: git merge --abort
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git merge --abort returns the project to its state before the merge.

flashcards.front: After you rebase a branch onto a newer main, do its commits keep their hashes? Why?
flashcards.back: No. Each replayed commit has a new parent, and the parent's hash is part of its content, so every one gets a new hash.

flashcards.front: Which interactive rebase action folds a commit into the one above it?
flashcards.back: squash combines the commit's changes with the one above and gives one commit.

acceptedIdeas: squash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: squash combines the commit's changes with the one above and gives one commit.

flashcards.front: Why is it risky to rebase commits you have already pushed and others have pulled?
flashcards.back: Rebase replaces them with copies that have new hashes, so the others' histories diverge from yours.

flashcards.front: Which git command makes a new commit that reverses an earlier commit?
flashcards.back: git revert adds a commit that applies the opposite change.

acceptedIdeas: git revert
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git revert adds a commit that applies the opposite change.

flashcards.front: You committed too early and the commit is only on your machine. How do `reset --soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` differ in what they leave of its changes?
flashcards.back: `--soft` leaves them staged, `--mixed` leaves them in the working tree unstaged, and `--hard` discards them.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the local record of where HEAD has been?
flashcards.back: The reflog, which lists earlier positions such as `HEAD@{1}`.

acceptedIdeas: reflog
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reflog, which lists earlier positions such as HEAD@{1}.

flashcards.front: How many tests, at most, does bisect need for a history of 1,000,000 commits?
flashcards.back: 2^20 is 1,048,576, so twenty halvings are enough.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^20 is 1,048,576, so twenty halvings are enough.

flashcards.front: Which exit code tells git bisect run that a commit is good?
flashcards.back: Exit code 0, the usual code for success.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero, the usual code for success.

flashcards.front: Why does git bisect need a test that gives the same answer every time?
flashcards.back: One wrong answer sends the search into the wrong half, so the commit it reports cannot be trusted.

flashcards.front: Which command downloads commits from the remote without changing your branch?
flashcards.back: git fetch updates origin/main and leaves your branch and files alone.

acceptedIdeas: git fetch
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: git fetch updates origin/main and leaves your branch and files alone.

flashcards.front: Why can origin/main be out of date?
flashcards.back: It is a bookmark that moves only when you fetch, pull or push, so it shows the host as it was at your last contact.

flashcards.front: You rebased a branch you had already pushed. Which `git push` option replaces it, and why is it safer than `--force`?
flashcards.back: `--force-with-lease` replaces the branch only if the host still points where your `origin/main` says, so it will not drop a commit pushed since your last fetch.

flashcards.front: Which practice merges small changes to a single main branch at least daily?
flashcards.back: Trunk-based development, with very short branches and feature flags.

acceptedIdeas: trunk-based development
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Trunk-based development, with very short branches and feature flags.

flashcards.front: Give one reason small pull requests are easier to review and safer to merge.
flashcards.back: Less to read, fewer conflicts, and one change is easy to revert alone.

flashcards.front: What do hosting services call the request to merge a branch, reviewed on a web page?
flashcards.back: A pull request, or in GitLab a merge request.

acceptedIdeas: pull request
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pull request, or in GitLab a merge request.

flashcards.front: Which Git object type does an annotated tag create, as reported by `git cat-file -t`?
flashcards.back: An annotated tag is its own object, so the type is tag.

acceptedIdeas: tag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An annotated tag is its own object, so the type is tag.

flashcards.front: What does each number of a semantic version tell a user?
flashcards.back: Major means a breaking change, minor means a compatible feature, and patch means a compatible fix.

flashcards.front: From 2.4.1, which version follows a breaking change?
flashcards.back: A breaking change raises the major number and resets the others to zero, which gives 3.0.0.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A breaking change raises the major number and resets the others to zero.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 10.3: Git References
sources.notes: The files under .git/refs/heads, the HEAD file and its ref: line, and lightweight against annotated tags as objects.

sources.title: gitglossary manual page
sources.section: Entries for detached HEAD, HEAD, branch, fast-forward, merge base and object name
sources.notes: Defines the detached HEAD state the branches lesson describes.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 3.2: Basic Branching and Merging
sources.notes: Fast-forward, the three-way merge from the common ancestor, the merge commit with more than one parent, and conflict markers and how to resolve them.

sources.title: git-merge manual page
sources.section: Options (--ff, --no-ff, --ff-only, --abort); Fast-forward merge; True merge; How conflicts are presented
sources.notes: The fast-forward options, the conflict marker layout and git merge --abort.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 3.6: Rebasing
sources.notes: How a rebase replays commits on a new base, that the result has the same snapshot as a merge, and the rule not to rebase commits others have.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 7.6: Rewriting History
sources.notes: Interactive rebase: the list in oldest-first order and the pick, reword and squash actions.

sources.title: git-rebase manual page
sources.notes: What git rebase does to the current branch, and the interactive commands.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 2.4: Undoing Things
sources.notes: git restore and git restore --staged, and that discarding an uncommitted edit cannot be undone.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 7.7: Reset Demystified
sources.notes: The three steps of reset: move the branch (--soft), update the index (--mixed, the default), update the working directory (--hard).

sources.title: git-revert manual page
sources.notes: Revert records new commits that reverse the effect of earlier ones.

sources.title: git-reflog manual page
sources.notes: What the reflog records, that it is local, and the default expiry of 90 days, or 30 days for unreachable entries.

sources.title: git-bisect manual page
sources.notes: The good and bad commands and the exit codes bisect run reads: 0 good, 1 to 127 except 125 bad, 125 skip.

sources.title: git-log manual page
sources.notes: The pickaxe lists commits that change the number of occurrences of a string.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 2.5: Working with Remotes
sources.notes: The name origin, fetching, pulling and pushing, and a push being rejected until you fetch the other work first.

sources.title: Pro Git, 2nd edition, section 3.5: Remote Branches
sources.notes: Remote-tracking branches such as origin/master, which move only when you contact the remote.

sources.title: git-pull manual page
sources.notes: git pull runs git fetch and then integrates. By default it only fast-forwards and fails on diverged branches; --no-rebase runs git merge and --rebase runs git rebase.

sources.title: git-push manual page
sources.notes: Why a push that is not a fast-forward is refused, and what --force-with-lease checks.
